newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: India PM seeks firmer trade ties with Bangladesh.
newsitem.headline: India PM seeks firmer trade ties with Bangladesh.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Tuesday proposed a long-term trade partnership with Bangladesh and gave assurances that more Bangladeshi goods would find a home in the Indian market.

"I firmly believe it is high time for us to put aside our political differences and work together to improve the lot of the millions of poor people in South Asia," he said in an address to Bangladeshi business leaders in Dhaka.
"I hope this vision is also driving business sectors in Bangladesh and look forward to establishing a long-term partnership between our two countries," the Indian premier said.
"It is my firm conviction that trade and economic relations provide the foundation for stable relations in all other fields."

Gowda arrived on Monday on a two-day visit to Bangladesh, less than a month after the two countries ended a decades-old dispute by signing an accord to share water from the Ganges River, which flows through both India and Bangladesh.
Officials in Dhaka said the visit would help cement relations after Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and Deve Gowda signed the 30-year Ganges treaty in New Delhi in December.
"I am sure that the concessions offered by India to Bangladesh will lead to substantially increased trade flows to India from Bangladesh," Gowda said.
Under the recent South Asian Preferential Trade Agreement, concessions were exchanged on nearly 2,000 items, with India providing concessions on 911 items, Gowda said.

A large number of the concessions given by India include items of interest to Bangladesh exporters and cover a variety of consumer goods, especially in the textiles, leather, cosmetics and table-ware sectors, he added.
The concessions are effective from March 1997.

Referring to the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), which groups India, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, Deve Gowda said: "It should be India and Bangladesh that are setting the pace for intensified regional cooperation."

Yussuf Abdullah Harun, President of the Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry, said Deve Gowda's visit would pave the way for enhanced cooperation, especially for trade, industry and investment through the private sector.
"We can at last put behind us the years of indifference which drove us to look to the West instead of drawing strength from each other," he said.
Harun referred to a huge trade imbalance in India's favour and urged New Delhi to give Bangladeshi goods greater access by cutting tariff rates and removing barriers.
In 1995/96 (July-June), Bangladesh imported $1.1 billion in goods from India but exports were a paltry $70 million, officials said.
